CHANGELOG.md:33:- A CAN broker refusal test no longer gives a spawning attach four seconds to start a broker, load the authoritative configuration, take the bus lock, spawn a bridge and spend the full second the fixture gives the adapter before printing its refusal: under load the client's own deadline expired first, terminated the broker it was waiting for and handed the test the terminate's exit code where the adapter exit was expected, so a loaded runner read as a defect in the code under test. The attach takes the product's own start timeout, which costs a healthy run nothing because this path ends the moment the broker exits with an explained code and never on the clock, and the refusal is timed against half that timeout, a product envelope rather than a scaled bound, so a broker that hangs instead of exiting is still read as a failure at every value of the suite's time scale factor. A walk over the suite's own source refuses any attach that may start a broker and bounds that start below half the product default, reads the number behind a module constant and behind `scaled_time_bound` so the same four seconds cannot return under another spelling, and names one by one the attaches whose refusal is decided before anything is waited for (#530)
CHANGELOG.md:73:- A COM port a POSIX system refuses to open for this user now says which group to join, `dialout` on Debian and Ubuntu, `uucp` on Arch and Fedora, and that a udev rule or the node's mode can deny it too; an attach whose CAN broker exits on an adapter it cannot open or a configuration it cannot read ends with the broker's own error type, summary and log instead of another respawn; and a device the configuration does not declare is named by the refusal it really gets, `unknown_device` to a run that declares it, `com_port_not_configured` or `can_bus_not_configured` to a port or a bus tool. (#508)

content.text:
The CAN broker is implemented in **`src/agentic_hil/canbroker.py`**.

This module defines the broker process that lets several participants (runs/processes) share one physical CAN bus: an entry in the config's `can_buses` with a `shares:` section names participant views (identifier filter, permissions, frame budget), and a single broker process owns the physical adapter plus the machine-wide bus lock (via `BenchMutex`), serializing access for all attached participants. Key pieces:

- The module docstring (`src/agentic_hil/canbroker.py:8-39`) explains the design: a bus with no `shares:` remains single-owner (no broker), the broker holds the same lock everyone else would have held, and attach uses an HMAC handshake so a client can prove it's talking to the right broker.
- The broker class itself lives around `src/agentic_hil/canbroker.py:504` onward (the section labeled "The broker"), handling the bus lock (`hold_bus_lock`/`BenchMutex`), attach/detach of participants, message dispatch (`attach`, `send`, `bus_status`), and per-bus frame/incident logging.

The client-side integration point is in **`src/agentic_hil/can.py`** (around line 718-723 and 1039), which calls into `canbroker.listen_only_proof`, `canbroker.share_view`, and `canbroker.attach_participant` only when a bus is brokered.

This is also documented in `CHANGELOG.md` (#146): "A CAN broker lets several runs share one physical bus: a `shares:` section under a `can_buses` entry names participant views (identifier filter, permissions, frame budget), and one broker process owns the adapter and the machine-wide bus lock for all of them."
